title: Chapter 54 – Pebble Taken
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

He wakes at the third hour of the night with his hand on nothing.

It is a small thing. His fingers are curled, as they have been curled every night for four months, round a warm round weight in the crook of his arm. They close on the quilt. He lies still, with his eyes open and the dark pressing down, and for a long moment he does not know what is wrong.

Then he knows.

Pebble.

There is no answer. He reaches for the bond, the thin warm thread that has run between them since the forest, and finds it. It is there. It is taut. But it is not slack and drowsy as it is in sleep. It is stretched, like a rope with a weight at the end of it, and the weight is moving.

He is out of bed before he has finished the thought.

* * *

The room is empty. The window is open.

It is a small casement, set high in the wall, that he has never opened because Pebble could not reach the sill. Tonight there is a stool under it. There is a wet print, round and small, on the stool's top. There is, on the sill itself, a faint clear smear, like the track of a snail, and a smell that makes him stop dead with one hand on the frame.

It is the smell of the Orchard. Of black earth after rain. Of crushed mint and tomato leaf. It is not strong. It is very faint, a trace, a ghost of a scent, but it is the one thing in the world that would draw her out of a sleeping house in the middle of a night, over a window sill four feet above the floor, without a sound.

Mother, he thinks. Pebble's mother.

Someone has put the smell of her mother on the sill.

He does not breathe. He stands in the dark with the cool night wind on his face and his heart going like a drum, and the whole of his mind, in a single sharp cold instant, turns to ice.

They knew. They knew what she would answer to.

He puts his thumb to the thread. Pebble. Pebble. Answer me.

For a long time there is nothing. Then, very faint, very small, across a great distance, a whisper:

Smell. Mother's smell. It was a good one. I thought, I will only look.

Where are you?

In the dark. A tiny, shaken pause. There is a cage. It is cold. It smells of dead things. A flutter, like the beat of a bird's wing against a wall. Jian, I think I made a mistake.

* * *

He does not wake his parents.

He thinks about it. He stands in the passage outside their door, in his stocking feet, with his boots in one hand and a needle roll in the other, and listens to his father's slow breathing on the other side of the paper wall. He thinks of what he would say. He thinks of how long it would take. He thinks of the thread, humming in his head, and the distance, which is a thing he can feel as a man feels a stone in his shoe. It is not far. It is perhaps a half-mile. And it is growing, steadily, in the direction of the north slope.

It will take me a quarter of an hour to explain, he thinks. And twenty minutes to arm a guard, and ten to find a lantern. And in that half hour she will be gone.

He is not proud of the next thing he does, which is to stand there a moment longer than he needs to, with his forehead against the paper wall, and let himself be ten. It lasts three breaths. Then he straightens, because someone has to, and nobody else is awake.

He puts the note on the floor, under the door, in a small hurried hand.

Gone to the quarry. Pebble taken. Do not follow alone. Bring Father's talismans. —J.

It is an inadequate note. It is also, he thinks, a perfectly honest one. He pulls on his boots and goes out into the night.

* * *

The hill is asleep. He goes down the back stair, past the kitchen garden, through the little gate in the wall that the cook uses for deliveries, and out onto the north slope, in a gray cloak, with the Veil drawn close. The night is thin and clear, and cold for summer. Stars are out in thousands. A sliver of old moon is hanging low over the pines. The grass is silver with dew.

He runs.

He is a fast runner. It is something he did not know about himself until the last month, when the Seed began to eat, and the Orchard air began to leave, and he found that a body made lean by a fifth of its own gain was a body made light. He goes up the quarry road in a dozen long strides, with the thread pulling at him like a hooked line, and the night wind in his teeth.

He thinks of Hu on the ridge, that noon, with the white bone arm in his lap. He does not threaten. When he says a thing is a pity, he has already decided. He had been told. He had been told in plain words, by a man who had known Mu for fifty years, and he had put the pangolin to bed in the crook of his arm and shut the casement latch, and gone to sleep. He had not thought of the stool.

That is the part he will not forgive. It is not the theft. It is the stool.

Level 2 Scan, he thinks, with a dry, clear fury that surprises him. Residue.

```
[ARK-7 — SCAN]
Trail detected: Organic residue on slope path (fresh).
1. Seamwalker (juvenile). Gait: slow. Hesitation at 3 points.
2. Human, adult female. Gait: even, stiff-legged. Does not
sweat. Does not breathe. Temperature: 4.1 C.
3. Blood salt (Drip marrow signature). Trace at 11 points.
Source of lure: vial, glass, discarded at the base of the east wall.
Contents: Seamwalker maternal pheromone (synthetic).
Method: Fabrication, hand-compounded. Skill: high.
```

Does not breathe.

He reads the second line twice. A dull cold prickle goes up his spine. He knows the signature of a dead body. He knows, too, that a dead body does not leave a trail of footprints on a dewed slope, that it does not step round a root, or turn aside from a pit, or stop at three points on a path out of what looks, from the print, like a human hesitation. Something is walking. Something that does not breathe is carrying his friend through the night.

Blood salt, he thinks. A Drip's marrow. A Drip's body.

And he understands, in a long cold spasm, exactly what has been done.

Mei Lian.

The elder sister. The one whose body Shan carried from the Narrows, in a cart, to Three Willows, to be burned in the Sect fashion with a drop of blood and a bow. He had promised, in the green hush of the Orchard, with her twin lying dying at his feet. We will find her. He had not known where to begin.

Mu has begun for him.

* * *

The seam is open when he reaches the quarry.

It stands at the foot of the east wall, where it has stood before, a long vertical line of green light, taller than a man. But it is not the clean thread of the first night. It is jagged. The edges are ragged and shuddering, as if torn by something clumsy, and a thin dry hiss comes from it, like cloth being slowly ripped. Around the foot of the wall the gravel is scuffed. There is a long smear of blood, and a small circle of white powder, and in the dust, quite distinct, the print of a bare, narrow, womanly foot.

Jian stands very still. He is breathing hard. He has run a mile in four minutes, with a rib that has not entirely mended, and the Seed is gnawing at him, a small dull pain in the belly, like hunger.

They opened it by force.

He knows it as a physician knows the breaking of a bone. The seam is not Pebble's. She opens them smoothly, with a gesture of pure will. This one has been wrenched. It has been cut, from outside, by someone who understands the thread of a seam and has found a way to drag it open. There is a ring of Coral Gate script scratched round the gravel in a double circle, in white chalk, in a clear sharp hand.

A key, he thinks. It is not a key. It is only a hook.

Behind him, the pines whisper. Far off a night bird calls, once, long and low. He is alone.

There is a thing he should do. He knows it. It is on the tip of his tongue like a name. He should go back down the hill and wake his father, and a dozen guards. The Bell can open a seam of its own, but only from within, and he is on the wrong side of it. He should wait for dawn, and a plan. It is the sane thing.

But the Orchard has no other door from this side, and the seam is closing.

He can see it. Even as he looks, a ragged edge flickers, narrows by a hair. A quarter of an hour, he thinks. Ten minutes. Before it knits itself shut and takes with it the only thread by which she can be found.

Pebble.

Here, says the thin small voice in the back of his head. It is very faint. It is almost gone. Cold. Cold. It is going the wrong way. It is going down.

He tightens his belt. He checks the needle roll. He thinks, for one swift clean instant, of his father's face, the long, tired, kindly face at the table in the study; and of his mother, in a small bright kitchen, with flour on her hands, saying You will tell me everything.

I am sorry, he thinks. I will tell you. I will tell you the moment it is over.

He steps into the seam.

* * *

It does not part for him. That is the first thing.

It is the Orchard's own door, and it has always opened like a mouth. Tonight it is a wound. He has to push. The green light is thick as treacle. It clings to his arms, his face, his lips, and it is bitter, with a taste like old pennies, and he has the dreadful clear sense, as he forces his shoulder through, of a thing that does not wish to be passed.

It lets him through anyway, with a sound like tearing silk.

He falls. He lands on his knees on the moss, gasping, with his hands in cold wet green, and the whole world is wrong.

The light is wrong. It is dim, and thick, and red. It has none of the pearly softness of the first night, nothing of the delicate drift of motes. The air is full of a fine pink haze, like the steam from a butcher's block. The moss under his hands is spongy with something that is not water.

The silence is wrong. He has never heard the Orchard silent. It has always had a voice, a low slow hum of root and water, a patient murmur at the edge of hearing. Now there is nothing. It is the silence of a held breath.

And the Wardens are wrong.

He sees them, at the end of the first row, in the red gloom. Four of them. They are standing exactly where he left them, in their ring, but their lamps are out. The green is gone from their faces. They are dull dead wood, and gray stone, and bark. A thin black thread of something, as fine as a hair, runs from the chest of each one down into the moss, and from the moss, away, in a long straight line, toward the far end of the garden, where the pool lies.

Blood thread, he thinks. They have bound them.

Not bound, says the interface, in a flat white line that wakes at the corner of his eye. Overwritten.

```
[ARK-7 — NOTICE]
Formation lattice: compromised.
Overwriting agent: BLOOD (Drip marrow, Pool-grade binder).
Wardens 1-11: DORMANT.
Gate Warden: status unknown.
Reservoir: no signal.
Orchard Qi: depleted 40% in last 11 minutes.
Hostile presence: 1 (at reservoir). Not living.
```

Not living.

He gets to his feet. He wipes his hands on his cloak. They leave a long pink smear. He draws the needle roll from his sleeve, with fingers that do not tremble, and takes out three.

Pebble, he says. I am here.

For a long moment there is nothing. Then, from a long way off, thin and clear as a struck glass, comes a single note. Not a word. A feeling. It is a flood of such unbearable relief, and shame, and love, that it very nearly drives him to his knees a second time.

I knew, she says. I knew you would come. I said so. I said, he is slow, but he comes.

I am not slow.

You are a little slow.

He laughs. It is an odd, cracked, helpless sound in the red silence, and he claps a hand over his mouth. Then he begins to walk.

* * *

The gate Warden is still standing.

He nearly passes it. It is at the foot of the broad black steps, in the red gloom, where it has stood since the first night, with its great granite shield on its arm. It has not moved. But its lamp is not out. It is a dim, small, flickering thing, a coal at the bottom of a cold hearth, and it is turned, very slightly, toward him.

A hundred threads of black hair run from its body into the moss. They cross and recross its limbs. They bind its knees and its elbows and its neck, and at each joint, where the old basalt has cracked, they have sunk into the stone like roots into a wall. It is straining. He can see the strain, in the tremor along the shield-arm, in the faint dry grinding of its jaw. It has been fighting for eleven minutes, with the whole of its three-hundred-year patience, to lift a single hand.

"I am here," Jian says.

The lamp flickers. The great head tilts a quarter-inch, with a sound like a tree in a wind.

It says, go, says Pebble, faint and far. It says, it cannot. It says, the thorn has come in by the window.

"I know."

It says... a gardener must not be late.

He stands for a moment longer, with his hand on the cold granite of its shield. It is warm, very faintly. It is the warmth of a hearth when the fire has gone out, but the stones remember.

"I will not be," he says.

He goes on.

* * *

The herb beds are dead.

He sees it as he goes, down the long avenue between the rows. The tall dark plants stand as they did, in their ring of white stones, but the silver has gone out of their leaves. They are limp. They are gray. At the foot of each, around the stem, a fine web of rust-colored thread lies on the earth, like the roots of a mold. It is drinking. He can feel it, through the soles of his boots, a long slow insidious suck, like a mouth at a straw.

The Orchard is being emptied.

It is the cost, he thinks, in a numb clear way, that he has been waiting for. He had thought it would come from the hill. He had thought it would come as a slow drain, over years, through the roots of the old vein, and had planned for that. He had not planned for a theft. Mu has not come to open the door. He has come to milk it. He has sent a dead girl and a vial of perfume, and he is draining the garden, bed by bed, into some vessel in the dark, because the door under the pool will want a great deal of Qi when it is finally unlocked.

And Pebble is the lock.

He quickens his pace. A cold sweat is running down his back. At the end of the avenue the pearl-gray stone of the terrace shows through the haze, and beyond it, the broad pale glimmer of the pool. It is not green. It is not lit. It is a flat, dark, sullen red, like a dish of old blood.

And on the near rim, on the low white wall, quite still, a woman is sitting with her back to him and a cage on her knees.

* * *

She is small. That is the first thing he sees.

She is very thin, and very straight, in a rust-colored cloak that has been mended, and mended again, at the hem. Her hair is black and long, tied in a plain knot at the nape. Her hands, in her lap, are long and pale. A black iron cage sits on her thighs, a squat box with bars of bone and etched with a tight repeating knot, and in it, curled in a ball with her scaled tail over her nose, is a small gray-white creature that is shaking from nose to tail.

Pebble does not look up. Her whole body is a thing of fear.

"Mei Lian," says Jian.

It is not loud. His voice does not carry. But the woman's head turns, slowly, with a small dry click, like a hinge. She looks at him over her shoulder.

It is her face. It is very like the one he saw at the Narrows, laughing, on the road. It has the same wide cheekbones, the same slim straight nose. But it has been kept. The skin is waxy and smooth. The lips are a faint, pearly, lavender color. There is a long clean cut under the collarbone, where Wenqing's pruning knife went in, and it has been stitched, neatly, with black silk thread. And her eyes are open, and dry, and quite empty, and in the red gloom they shine like the eyes of an animal at the edge of a fire.

"Good evening, little boy," she says.

It is not her voice. It is a husk of it, a dry flat sound, like a voice read aloud from a paper. But the words are quite distinct. And behind them, very faintly, like the hum of a bee in a bottle, he can hear a second voice, gentle and mild and warm.

Good evening, little boy, it says, through her. I told you that I should like to see you.

Jian does not move. In his right hand, three needles are lifted, quivering, on their thread. In his left, there is a handful of cold air. He looks at the dead woman, and at the cage, and at the red pool behind her, and a very small, very quiet part of him, the part that counts, says, in a tone of perfect dry detachment: There is a Pool-stage cultivator forty miles away, who has put a thread into the body of a corpse, and is speaking through it, and is waiting for you to be afraid.

"Elder Mu," he says.

The dead lips curve. It is an awful, tender, delicate smile.

"It is a pleasure to meet you at last," says Mu, in the mouth of Mei Lian. "I have heard so much. I am afraid you have caught me at a poor moment. I had meant to do this in a more courteous way." The thin white hand lifts, and strokes, with one finger, the black iron bars of the cage. "But you will understand that I had very little time. And I find that the pangolin is a remarkably stubborn child."

Jian, says Pebble, in the dark of his skull. It is a whisper. Do not listen. Do not. He is not kind. He only sounds it.

"I know," says Jian, quietly, to both.

"I should like to explain," says Mu, in the dead woman's dry voice. "It is only courteous. You have come a long way, and I should hate you to think I am a cruel man." The thin pale head tilts. "A seamwalker opens doors. It is the whole of what she is. In her lifetime she may open perhaps a dozen. Each costs her a scale, and a great many years of strength. And at the very end of her life, when there is nothing left to lose, she opens one door that no other creature in the world can. It is called the Last Seam. It is the only thing that will unlock the vault under this pool."

A coin, thinks Jian. Hu said. You keep it, and use it once, at the end.

"She is very young," says Mu, with real regret. "I had hoped to wait. I would have waited ten years, in a better world. But my master is dying, and the pool is draining, and I find that I have not ten days." The mild voice drops. "She will open it for me tonight. She will not open another. I am very sorry. I think she is a most remarkable child."

"You will kill her."

"I will use her. It is a different thing. I am told it is not painful."

It is, says Pebble, very small. It is a little.

Something white and hard and perfectly clear goes through Jian's mind. It is not rage. He has been angry before. It is a great quiet clarity, like the stillness at the center of a storm, and in it he sees, quite distinctly, the whole of the board: the dead woman, the cage, the red pool, the three needles on their threads, and a gap, small and exact, in the wall of the sister's Qi at the join of the shoulder, where a stitched cut has never quite closed.

She is a Drip, he thinks. She is QR8, even dead. She has a thread in her. It runs to him. A thread can be cut.

He draws a long breath. In the red haze, in the silent garden, with the whole of the Orchard dying round his feet and his friend in a cage and an old man's voice speaking out of a dead girl's mouth, he feels something very still and very cold settle in the middle of his chest. It is not fear. It is something he has not felt since the forest. It is the sense, perfectly precise, of a door closing behind him, and a long dark corridor ahead, and a single light at the end.

"Mei Lian," he says. "I promised your sister that I would find you."

For a moment the dead face does not change.

Then, very slowly, for the first time, something moves behind the empty eyes. It is quick. It is small. It is gone before he can name it. It is, he thinks, the faintest, farthest ghost of a woman, drowned deep in her own corpse, turning her head in the dark to hear a name.

"Yes," says Mu, gently, in her voice. "You did, didn't you? That was very kind. I shall see that she hears of it."

The hands tighten on the cage. The red pool behind her begins, quite silently, to boil. A single bubble rises, fat and slow, and breaks on the surface with a sound like a swallowed word; and in the shuddering light the cage on the dead woman's knees gives a thin, high, metallic whine, and the small pale thing inside it cries out.
